topic: maturing alpine cheese wheels in a cellar cave and fixing cracked rinds

provenance.author: glowny-en-a
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is ledger arithmetic on the same cheese makes with closed task questions, base is a diagnosis of cracked rinds in the maturing cellar. Grounded external referent: the cave, introduced in turn 0 and carried through the whole diagnosis (it holds the shelves, its vent and humidity are the suspects, wheels rotate through its corners).

a: Here are five cheese batches for the ledger, and their wheel counts need adding in order.
The March make has twelve wheels and the April make has nine wheels on record.
The May make has seven wheels, and the June make has six wheels on the same page.
The July make is the smallest entry of the five at four wheels in total.
How many wheels do the five makes come to when every entry is added together?
base: Our alpine wheels have started cracking along the rind about six weeks into their stay underground.
We mature everything in the cave behind the dairy, a cellar cut into the hillside years ago.
The cave holds forty wheels on chestnut shelves, and the oldest rounds sit nearest the door.
Lately the young wheels dry out at the edge while their centres stay soft and springy.
Where would you begin looking for the fault before we lose the autumn batch as well?

a: Added in order, the running counts are twelve, then twenty-one, then twenty-eight wheels so far.
The last two entries bring the count to thirty-four and then thirty-eight wheels in all.
At nine kilograms apiece, the March make weighs one hundred eight kilograms on the scale.
The April make weighs eighty-one kilograms at that same rate of nine kilograms for every wheel.
Does the full count of thirty-eight wheels match the number on the cellar door sheet?
base: Cracked rinds that early usually point to dry air rather than anything wrong with the curd.
A young wheel wants humidity above ninety percent, and a draught can undo that in hours.
Chestnut shelves drink moisture as well, so fresh boards can pull water straight out of cheese.
I would hang a wet and dry gauge in the cave at shelf height near the door.
Do you notice whether the cracking is worse on the door side than at the back?

a: Now work out the brine for each make at four litres for every ten wheels.
List the brine for all five makes in the March to July order given above.
Salt goes into each tub at three hundred grams for every litre of brine mixed.
Put the March and April tubs on row one, and the other three on row two.
Which brine volume belongs to the May make at that fixed rate of four litres?
base: The cracking is clearly worse near the door, and the back rows look almost untouched.
The cave has a single vent above the door, and it stays open through most days.
We brush the shelves weekly, but the boards nearest the entrance always feel dry to the hand.
The gauge we borrowed read eighty-two percent by the door and ninety-four at the far wall.
Would closing that vent for part of the day be enough to even things out?

a: The March make takes four point eight litres of brine at the stated rate.
The April make takes three point six litres, and the May make takes two point eight.
The June make takes two point four litres, and the July make takes one point six.
Row one therefore carries eight point four litres across its two tubs in total.
Row two carries six point eight litres, and the salt for it weighs two point zero four kilograms.
base: Closing the vent at midday would help, though you would trade dryness for stale air.
Moving the youngest wheels to the far wall is the cheaper fix, and it works at once.
Wheels under eight weeks need the damp corner, while older rounds can stand the drier row.
You could also lay wet burlap over the door racks and rinse it every second morning.
Swapping shelf rows weekly keeps every wheel through the same corners of the cave in turn.

a: One correction before anything else: the June make holds seven wheels, not six as written.
Recalculate its weight and its brine, and leave the other four makes exactly as they stand.
Then give the new totals for wheels and for brine across all five makes together.
After that, list the makes in the order they leave for the buyer next spring.
Which make leaves first under the order March, then May, then April, then June, then July?
base: We moved the young wheels back and hung the burlap the way you described this morning.
Two of the cracked rounds have grown a grey bloom inside the split since last week.
The bloom wipes off easily, but it returns within a day or two on the same wheels.
Our notebook says nothing like this appeared in the last three seasons of records we keep.
Should we cut those two wheels open now or let them ride until the usual tasting?

a: With seven wheels the June make weighs sixty-three kilograms at nine kilograms for each wheel.
Its brine becomes two point eight litres, and its salt eight hundred forty grams exactly.
The new wheel total is thirty-nine, and the new brine total is fifteen point six litres.
The leaving order stands as March first, then May, then April, then June, then July last.
The March make therefore ships first, and the July make closes out the spring deliveries.
base: Grey bloom in a fresh crack is common mould, and wiping alone will never keep it away.
Rub the split with strong brine, then dry salt, and press the faces closed under a board.
Keep those two on the lowest shelf of the cave where the air moves least of all.
Check them every second day for a fortnight, and mark each visit in the notebook.
If the split keeps opening past a finger's depth, cut both wheels and use them young.

a: Convert the full thirty-nine wheels into crates that hold six wheels in each crate.
Tell me how many full crates that makes and how many wheels ride in the open crate.
Then split the brine total into two tubs of equal volume and give each figure.
The delivery van pulls away at half past eight with crates loaded ten minutes apart.
How many full crates do thirty-nine wheels come to at six wheels for every crate?
base: The brine and salt held, and the splits have stopped spreading on both marked wheels.
The gauge now reads ninety-one percent by the door since the burlap went up on the racks.
Our buyer wants sixty wheels by spring, which is twenty more than the shelves have carried.
There is room for two more racks along the back wall if we build them narrow.
Would crowding the racks that tightly set the humidity swinging out of balance again?

a: Thirty-nine wheels make six full crates with three wheels left over for the open crate.
Each of the two tubs holds seven point eight litres of brine when split evenly.
The first crate loads at seven and the second crate loads at seven ten.
The third loads at seven twenty, the fourth at seven thirty, the fifth at seven forty.
The sixth crate loads at seven fifty, and the open crate follows at eight exactly.
base: Crowding helps humidity if anything, because more cheese means more moisture breathing into the room.
The real risk is still air pocketing between racks, which invites the wrong moulds to settle.
Leave a hand's width between the new racks and the wall so air can climb behind them.
Put the older rounds up high and keep the young wheels low where it stays damp.
A small vent at floor level opposite the door would give the whole room a gentle loop.

a: Write out a four step loading sheet for the crew in the order given here.
Step one is crating, step two is weighing, step three is loading the van.
Step four is the paperwork, and every step needs its clock time on the sheet.
Crating begins at half past six and the van pulls away at half past eight.
Crating takes twenty minutes and weighing takes ten minutes for the whole spring set.
base: We will build the racks narrow and cut the low vent during the quiet week after Christmas.
My brother wants to keep a written turning rota so nothing depends on memory alone.
The notebook now lists every wheel with its make date, shelf row and last turning day.
Each Saturday we will swap rows, wipe boards and note the gauge readings twice over.
The spring batch should reach the buyer with even rinds if we hold to that rhythm.

a: Step one runs from half past six until ten to seven on the loading sheet.
Step two runs from ten to seven until seven, taking the ten minutes allowed.
Step three runs from seven until eight, which covers all seven crates ten minutes apart.
Step four runs from eight until quarter past eight, leaving fifteen minutes of slack in hand.
The van pulls away at half past eight with all thirty-nine wheels and the papers aboard.
base: That rota covers everything that went wrong this autumn, and it costs only an hour weekly.
Keep the door-side row for wheels past three months, since they can bear the drier air.
Taste one wheel from each make date monthly, and write a line about salt and texture.
When the new vent goes in, watch the gauge daily for the first fortnight afterwards.
By spring the room should run itself, with the records catching any drift before the cheese does.
